cards.text: This is a song of ascents from Solomon, king of Israel (1 Kings 2:12). He sings about a house going up and a city with watchmen standing guard. And he's got one big condition hanging over both of them.

cards.question: Builders can labor on a house all they want. Solomon says their labor is in vain unless what?

cards.text: Now the city. The watchmen stand guard with their eyes wide open, and I know that look, friend, because I wore it in the back of a junk drawer for YEARS.

cards.question: True or false: Solomon says the city is safe as long as the watchmen stand guard.

cards.text: Then Solomon turns to the worker who rises early and stays up late, toiling for bread to eat. That's a baker's schedule, and my oven timer is TIRED of me.

cards.question: Solomon says all that early rising and late toiling is in vain, for He gives ___ to His beloved.

cards.text: He gives SLEEP to His beloved, and friend, I have never felt so seen by a verse in my life. Then Solomon turns from houses and cities to children.

cards.question: Solomon calls children a heritage. Where does he say that heritage comes from?
True or false: Solomon calls the fruit of the womb the LORD's reward.
Solomon paints a picture of children born in one's youth. He says they're like what in the hand of a warrior?

cards.text: If children are arrows, then "Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them." Six cookie cutters, friend, my quiver was FULL, and Mags made sure the whole kitchen heard about it.

cards.question: Solomon says the man with a full quiver will not be put to shame. When?

answers.text: When he confronts enemies at the gate
When he stands before the king
When he brings his offering to the priest

cards.text: Next up is another song of ascents, and this one doesn't have a name on it. It's got work and family in it too. And it opens with a blessing.

cards.question: This song opens by calling someone blessed. Who?

answers.text: All who rise early to work

cards.text: Remember all that toiling in vain back in Psalm 127? Now this song talks about your labor too, and you get to eat its fruit.

cards.question: When you eat the fruit of your labor, what does this song say will be yours?

cards.text: Then the song walks right into the house and takes a look around the table.

cards.question: In this song, the wife is like something flourishing within the house. What is it?
True or false: The song pictures the sons like young cedars sitting around the table.

cards.text: Sons like olive shoots around the table, and my six sat around a mixing bowl with the EXACT same energy. Chip wanted one more story, and Mags wanted the whole kitchen to hear it.

cards.question: The song sums it up: In this way indeed shall ___ come to the man who fears the LORD.

cards.text: Then the song turns to you: "May the LORD bless you from Zion," and friend, that's the send-off I want stamped on every cookie box I seal.

cards.question: True or false: The song says this is so you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life.
There's one more thing the song says you may see. What is it?

cards.text: GRANDKIDS, and a long life to see them! Then the song closes with one last line for the whole nation: "Peace be upon Israel!"

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences. The 3-sentence allowance is for 'the opening card', and every other story card is limited to 1 to 2. This card starts a new psalm with its own superscription, so it does a similar job to an opening card.
findings.question: When a stop begins a new psalm (or a new section with its own heading) inside one passage, does its first story card get the up-to-3-sentence opening card allowance, or is that only for the walkthrough's first card?

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'Rest and quiet' is arguably true within the passage. Psalm 127:2 says 'He gives sleep to His beloved.' A baker could argue that rest is part of what the LORD gives.

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: 'Then the song turns to you' says the address changes at 128:5. It doesn't. The psalm has spoken to 'you' since 128:2 ('when you eat the fruit of your labor') and 128:3 ('Your wife... your sons... your table').

rule.text: Noticing: What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: The question says 'The song says this is so you may see...', but 'this' points back to the blessing from Zion on card 10, which is no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: 'GRANDKIDS, and a long life to see them!' turns a wish into a stated promise and adds 'a long life'. The text is a wish ('May the LORD bless you... that you may see your children's children'). 'All the days of your life' goes with seeing Jerusalem's prosperity, not with a promise of a long life.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Most of Stop 2 is mild. Cards 1, 3, 5 and 13 have almost no personality. Cards 8 and 10 read like a nice dad being pleasant rather than laugh-out-loud funny. Card 8 also reuses Stop 1 card 11's beat about Mags making the whole kitchen hear it.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
